title: Karna gives his armor
hookLine: the boy grows up worshipping the sun, and one morning a stranger asks him for the armor he was born in
carry: dana: giving, even when it costs
tomorrow: who in the crowd knows Karna?
last: VATSALYA: THE LOVE THAT RAISES A CHILD.

lines: HE FACES THE SUN EACH MORNING.
WHILE HE PRAYS, HE REFUSES NO BRAHMIN.
cards: Every morning the young man stands facing the sun, hands joined, praying, until the sun is high and its heat is on his back. That's Karna, grown. He doesn't know the sun is his father.
And the text adds a detail: while he prays, there's nothing he will refuse a Brahmin who asks. Today a stranger comes during that hour, and asks for the one thing Karna was born wearing.

teach.b: The stranger is dressed as a Brahmin, a priest. But the Mahabharata lets us in on the secret: he's Indra, king of the gods, and the father of Arjuna.
Indra knows that as long as Karna wears his armor and earrings, nobody can beat him, so he comes to ask for them as alms.
The Adi Parva tells this scene early, beside Karna's birth, though in the story's order it comes years later.

teach.h: THE SUN WARNS HIM IN A DREAM.
teach.b: In a later book, the sun himself warns Karna in a dream that Indra is coming, and tells him to refuse. Karna answers that he can't. He's vowed to give, and he'd rather lose his life than his name for giving.
So the sun tells him: then ask for Indra's dart in return. The Brahmin asks. Karna asks for the dart, a weapon that can kill one enemy, and Indra grants it.

teach.h: HE CUTS THE ARMOR FROM HIS BODY.
teach.b: Then Karna takes a blade, cuts the armor from his own body and the earrings from his ears, and hands them over. Here's the teaching Hindus hear in it.
Dana: giving, one of the oldest duties in Hindu life. The Gita calls the purest gift one given simply because giving is right, at the right time, to someone worthy, expecting nothing back.
Karna's gift isn't that pure; he bargains for a weapon, and guards his name. But he keeps his vow at the cost of his own protection.

teach.h: DANA: GIVING, EVEN WHEN IT COSTS.
teach.b: That's why popular tellings call him Daanveer Karna, the hero of giving, even though he'll fight on Duryodhana's side.

how: In Hindu storytelling Karna is remembered as Daanveer, the hero of giving; his gift of the armor to Indra is retold as the measure of keeping one's word to give, whatever it costs.

practice: Karna's day began facing the sun, hands joined. Many Hindus still greet the morning sun, Surya, by pouring a little water toward it, an offering called arghya, often with the Gayatri mantra. Turn toward whatever light is near you.
Then choose one small gift you'll give today, time, attention, something you own, and ask nothing back. If you don't pray, skip the water and keep the gift.

wordCard.voice: Karna's abandonment. The child set adrift grows into a man who gives away even his father's armor, cut from his own body, because someone asked.

orig.note: Sanskrit dāna: giving, a gift; one of the oldest duties in Hindu life.
